data.question: Can one script list and apply the five hand edits of a new event kind?

evidence.note: research note CONFIRMED: check agrees with the four ratchet tests on the tree (303 passed)

scripts/event_kind.py check/add, lenient read_log, tests/test_event_kind_scaffold.py; 399 selected tests passed

chunk_findings.detail: When a kind already has a `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS` entry, `add` still emits a *second* line for that same kind key. `text = [n for n in args.text if n not in text_fields.get(kind, ())]` (line 155) filters out fields already listed, but it does not consider that the kind key itself is already present, and `_insert` splices the new line directly after `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS: ... = {`, i.e. *before* the pre-existing entry. A Python dict literal with a duplicate key keeps the last occurrence, so the pre-existing (later) entry wins and the newly requested text field is silently dropped. Concrete input: a kind `lease.waiting` already mapped to `("reason",)`; run `scripts/event_kind.py add lease.waiting --why "..." --text detail`. The script prints `redact: LOG_TEXT_FIELDS lease.waiting ['detail']`, but the written literal is `{ "lease.waiting": ("detail",), ... "lease.waiting": ("reason",), ... }`, `literal_eval` (and the imported module) yields `("reason",)`, and the `check` pass that `main` runs immediately afterwards re-reads the file and reports `redact: field 'detail' is neither LOG_TEXT_FIELDS nor a lookup` — the exact failing-test round the tool exists to avoid. The stated contract ("it never edits an entry that exists") is also violated.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/event_kind.py:155-157 (`add`, LOG_TEXT_FIELDS insert)

chunk_findings.detail: `add` is not atomic: the fixture is rewritten at lines 149-153 (and `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS`/`LOG_VERBATIM_FIELDS` are spliced at 157/167) *before* the `--lookup` spec is validated at lines 162-163 and before the `--exempt` length check at lines 171-172. Input `scripts/event_kind.py add foo --why "w" --field x=str --exempt "too short"` raises `SystemExit("--exempt: say why in more than 20 characters")` only after the fixture entry for `foo` and the redact edits have been written to disk, leaving the repository half-scaffolded with no coherence entry or fragment; the user must hand-undo, which reintroduces the multi-round failure mode the script is meant to remove. Likewise `--lookup x` (no `=WHY`) aborts at line 163 with the fixture already modified.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/event_kind.py:141-172 (`add`, write-before-validate ordering)

chunk_findings.detail: The dedup for lookup fields only checks the on-disk set `taken`, never the `pairs` being accumulated, so a repeated option inserts the same `(kind, name)` key twice: `--lookup f=why1 --lookup f=why2` writes two identical-key lines into `LOG_VERBATIM_FIELDS`, and `literal_eval` (last-wins) keeps only `why2`, silently discarding the first reason.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/event_kind.py:164 (`add`, --lookup dedup)

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to verify that `check x.new` lists all five hand edits, but its loop is `("handler", "fixture", "coherence", "fragment")` and omits `redact`. Given the input `x.new` (a kind with no edits anywhere), if `event_kind.py check x.new` never emits the `x.new: redact:` line, this test still passes because only the other four substrings are asserted and the nonzero return code alone does not prove the redact edit was reported. That leaves the redact-listing capability, one of the five edits this change exists to surface, unverified at the only positive test for the “lists all of them” behavior.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_event_kind_scaffold.py::test_a_kind_with_no_edits_lists_all_of_them

chunk_findings.detail: The tolerance is applied only to the parse step, not to the read step. `p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` is evaluated in the `for` header, *outside* the `try`, so a half-written shard can still kill `--write` — with a different exception than the one the change targets. Concretely: if the worktree's `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl` is being appended to by a running ddflow while `--write` reads it, the bytes on disk can end in the middle of a UTF-8 sequence (the writer's 8 KiB block buffer can flush on a boundary that falls inside a multi-byte character, which is easy when payloads contain non-ASCII message text). `read_text` then raises `UnicodeDecodeError` before any line reaches `Event.from_json`, the `except (ValueError, KeyError, TypeError)` never runs, and `python tests/test_event_upcasters.py --write` still dies — exactly the failure mode the intent says must be tolerated. (Similarly `FileNotFoundError` if a shard is rotated away between `glob` and the read.) Reading with `errors="replace"` / opening and iterating inside the `try`, or wrapping the whole per-file read, is needed to actually deliver "tolerant of a half-written shard".
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_event_upcasters.py:103 (`read_log`)

chunk_findings.detail: The lenient path swallows far more than the torn-tail JSONDecodeError that motivated it: `KeyError` and `TypeError` from `Event.from_json` on a *complete* line are also skipped, and `_write` then goes on to overwrite the committed fixture with what it did observe. Input: a shard containing a well-formed JSON line for a kind whose upcaster chain does not yet know a newly required key (the very workflow this feature targets) — `from_json` raises `KeyError`, the line is printed to stderr and dropped, and line 660 writes `tests/fixtures/event_kinds.json` without that kind's fields while exiting 0. Before this change that line aborted the run *before* `FIXTURE.write_text`, so the fixture could not be silently corrupted; now the regenerated fixture can be missing kinds, and the omission surfaces later as an unrelated-looking coverage/upcaster failure. Restricting the skip to the final (possibly unterminated) line of each shard, or to `json.JSONDecodeError` only, keeps the intended tolerance without letting schema bugs rewrite the fixture.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_event_upcasters.py:657 (`_write` → `read_log(logs, lenient=True)`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_insert(REDACT, "LOG_TEXT_FIELDS:", [f"    {_q(kind)}: ({', '.join(map(_q, text))},),"])` inserts the new entry at the *top* of the `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS` dict literal (immediately after the opening line). If the kind already has an entry in that dict, the file now contains a duplicate key (`"kind": (...)` twice), and Python dict-literal semantics make the *later* entry win — i.e. the pre-existing entry shadows the newly inserted one. Reproduction: `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS` contains `"lease.waiting": ("note",)`; run `scripts/event_kind.py add lease.waiting --why "..." --field reason=str --text reason`. `text = [n for n in args.text if n not in text_fields.get(kind, ())]` is non-empty (`reason` is not in the existing tuple), so the command prints `redact: LOG_TEXT_FIELDS lease.waiting ['reason']` and reports success, but the re-run of `check` (same invocation) still reports `lease.waiting: redact: field 'reason' is neither LOG_TEXT_FIELDS nor a lookup`, because `_redact()` uses `ast.literal_eval` and the shadowing entry drops `reason`. The extension/re-run path is explicitly a supported use case ("it never edits an entry that exists"), and here it silently writes a no-op plus a duplicate key instead of merging the field into the existing tuple.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/event_kind.py — `add()` / `_insert()` for `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS`

chunk_findings.detail: Two validations run only after the fixture and `core/redact.py` have already been written: the `--lookup` `NAME=WHY` check inside the `for spec in args.lookup` loop, and the `len(args.exempt) <= MIN_REASON` check. Reproduction: `scripts/event_kind.py add foo --why "..." --field a=str --text a --exempt short` writes the `event_kinds.json` entry and inserts the `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS` line, then aborts with `SystemExit("--exempt: say why in more than 20 characters")`. The user sees a failure exit code and an error that says nothing was applied, while `tests/fixtures/event_kinds.json` and `ddflow/core/redact.py` have already been modified (and the fragment has not), leaving the tree half-applied. Validating `--lookup` and `--exempt` before the first `write_text`/`_insert` call would make the command all-or-nothing.
chunk_findings.location: scripts/event_kind.py — `add()` ordering of validation vs. writes
chunk_findings.title: scripts/event_kind.py — `add()` ordering of validation vs. writes

chunk_findings.detail: [D-small-files] This test file is already far past the 20 KB ceiling the decision imposes ("applies to tests as well as source"), and the change makes it larger instead of splitting it: it grows the module by a new keyword parameter, a multi-line docstring, a rewritten loop body, the `except`/`print` branch, and the extra `, lenient=True` call site, on top of a ~660-line file. The decision's remedy for a file over the limit is to split it into a package of smaller modules, so an edit of this size to this file should have moved `read_log`/the fixture-merge helpers into their own module rather than accreting more code here. Demonstrating the failure mode the decision targets: an agent asked to change upcaster/fixture behaviour must now load the whole ~660-line test module into context (log-reading, observation/merge, the exemption tables and the CLI entry point together) to make even this small edit.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_event_upcasters.py:657 (_write / read_log)

chunk_findings.detail: The change closes the superseded "write-before-validate" finding only for the three validation errors it loops over in `test_a_refused_add_writes_nothing` (`--exempt`, malformed `--lookup`, bad `--field`). The refusal raised when the kind already carries the requested field — the case this new test exercises — is asserted only with `pytest.raises(SystemExit)`: it never snapshots the tree, so it cannot distinguish "refused, nothing written" from "refused after writing". Concretely, run `python scripts/event_kind.py add bug.found --why w --text detail`; if the collision check (the code that replaced the duplicate-line bug) still sits in the phase that splices `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS`/rewrites `tests/fixtures/event_kinds.json`, i.e. *after* those writes, the command exits nonzero but leaves `ddflow/core/redact.py` (and possibly the fixture) modified — exactly the failure class the earlier review reported in this same function. Every new test still passes, including `test_a_refused_add_writes_nothing`, because that test's three inputs never reach the text-collision path. Adding the "already-listed field" input to `test_a_refused_add_writes_nothing`'s tuple (it already snapshots and compares the whole tree) is what would actually pin the atomicity of this path.

chunk_findings.detail: `table()` interpolates `k.doc` verbatim into a Markdown row: `f"| \`{k.name}\` | {k.owner} | {k.v} | {k.retention} | {k.doc} |"`. Nothing in `parse()` forbids `|` (or a newline, reachable via a TOML `"""…"""` string) in `doc`, and docs are free prose. Given an owner file with `doc = "Recorded when a vs b is chosen|reason"`, the generated docs row gains a sixth cell and the "what it records" column is shifted/garbled; a multi-line doc breaks the table row outright. The one deliverable of this change that consumes `table()` is the generated documentation, so the output is wrong for legal declarations.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/eventkinds.py:table

chunk_findings.detail: [r-everything-configurable] The intent states the conformance rule "every number is a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt", but this module adds `MIN_DOC = 10` as a bare constant used directly in `problems()` (`len(k.doc.strip()) < MIN_DOC`), with no file/CLI/MCP/prompt source and no override path; `RETENTIONS`/`_KEYS` are likewise fixed sets. An operator who wants a stricter or looser doc-length gate (e.g. per org) cannot set it, so the ratchet threshold is not configurable as required.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/eventkinds.py:MIN_DOC

chunk_findings.detail: `_declare` recreates the unreleased upgrade fragment for any kind whose `event_kind_added.<kind>.toml` is absent, with no `_released(kind)` guard, even though `check` right below treats that fragment as unnecessary for a released kind (`... and not _released(kind)`). This is reachable exactly through the workflow the new ratchet creates: once `check` prints `registry: declared in no ddflow/templates/events/<owner>.toml` for a kind that already shipped, the tool that fixes `check` output is `add`. Given a kind such as `task.created` that was released earlier (its fragment was folded into that release, so `_released("task.created")` is true and the file is gone), running `uv run scripts/event_kind.py add task.created --why "<long doc>"` takes the `if not frag.exists()` branch and writes a fresh `ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/event_kind_added.task.created.toml` (nothing else is needed if the registry row is already present). Since `check` only reports *missing* fragments, the extra file passes validation silently, and when the next version is cut the upgrade tooling folds it into that release and announces `event_kind_added` for a kind that had already shipped in an earlier version — a wrong changelog entry produced by the tool meant to keep the registry honest.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/event_kind.py:_declare

chunk_findings.detail:
`table()` interpolates `k.doc` (and `k.name`) straight into a Markdown row without escaping. The ratchet in `problems()` only enforces that a doc ends with a full stop (`k.doc.strip().endswith(".")`), so a declaration such as

```toml
[[kind]]
name = "lease.waiting"
doc = """Records the lease | holder.

Second line."""
```

passes `problems()` but `table()` emits `| \`lease.waiting\` | ... | Records the lease | holder. Second line. |`, which the Markdown parser reads as extra columns and a broken row. The same happens for a doc with an embedded `|` even on one line. Since the module's stated purpose includes producing the generated documentation table, a doc string that is legal by every check this file performs silently corrupts that output; either the ratchet should reject `|`/newlines in docs or `table()` should escape them.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/eventkinds.py:table()

chunk_findings.detail: The gate validates the *raw* why (`len(args.why.strip()) < MIN_DOC`) but then stores a *different*, normalized value (`args.why.strip().rstrip(".") + "."`). Because `rstrip(".")` removes every trailing dot and only one dot is added back, any input with two or more trailing dots passes the gate while producing a stored doc shorter than the advertised `MIN_DOC`. Concrete: with `MIN_DOC = 20`, `--why "...................."` (20 dots) has stripped length 20, so it passes the check, but normalization yields `"" + "."` = `"."`, and a one-character doc is written as the kind's documentation. Likewise `--why "$(printf 'a%.0s' {1..18}).."` (20 chars) passes and stores 19 chars, violating the stated "at least MIN_DOC characters" invariant. The check should be performed on the value actually persisted (after stripping/normalizing), or normalization should not be able to shorten the input below `MIN_DOC`.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/event_kind.py:193 (`args.why` validation vs. normalization)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new one-line guard is `if "|" in k.doc or "
" in k.doc.strip():` — it checks for newlines in the *stripped* doc. `str.strip()` removes leading/trailing whitespace, so a doc with a leading or trailing newline passes validation yet is still interpolated verbatim by `table()` as `f"| ... | {k.doc} |"`. Concretely, an owner file with `doc = """Records x.
"""` (TOML preserves the newline before the closing `"""`; a basic string `"Records x.
"` is equivalent) yields `k.doc == "Records x.
"`; `k.doc.strip()` is `"Records x."`, which ends with `.` and contains no newline, so `problems()` returns no line for this kind. The generated docs table then emits `| \`x.y\` | owner | 1 | keep | Records x.` followed by a stray ` |` line, which terminates the Markdown table — exactly the failure the guard was added to prevent. The same applies to a leading newline (`
Records x.`), and `` is likewise removed by `strip()`. The probe added for #1 (`test_a_doc_that_would_break_the_table_is_refused`) apparently exercises `|`, not this path, so it does not answer it.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new guard tests `"\n" in k.doc.strip()`, but the previous finding established that `table()` interpolates the *raw* `k.doc` into the Markdown row. Using `.strip()` before searching the string discards exactly the leading/trailing newlines that make the raw value unsafe, so a hand-written declaration such as

```toml
[[kind]]
name = "lease.waiting"
owner = "lease"
doc = """
Records the lease holder.
"""
```

yields `k.doc == "\nRecords the lease holder.\n"`. The existing full-stop check sees `"Records the lease holder."` and passes, and `"\n" in k.doc.strip()` is `False`, so `problems()` raises nothing; `table()` then emits a row with a newline before and after the cell, splitting one table row over three lines. (The same bypass applies to a lone `\r`, which `.strip()` also removes but which no check looks for.) The interior-newline probe added in the diff (`"Two\nlines."`) does not cover this case, so finding 1 is only partially answered: the guard would need to test the raw `k.doc` (`"\n" in k.doc or "\r" in k.doc`) or `table()` would need to render `k.doc.strip()`.

chunk_findings.detail: `table()` interpolates `k.doc` verbatim into a Markdown row: `f"| \`{k.name}\` | {k.owner} | {k.v} | {k.retention} | {k.doc} |"`. Nothing in `parse()` forbids `|` (or a newline, reachable via a TOML `"""…"""` string) in `doc`, and docs are free prose. Given an owner file with `doc = "Recorded when a vs b is chosen|reason"`, the generated docs row gains a sixth cell and the "what it records" column is shifted/garbled; a multi-line doc breaks the table row outright. The one deliverable of this change that consumes `table()` is the generated documentation, so the output is wrong for legal declarations.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/eventkinds.py:table

chunk_findings.detail: [r-everything-configurable] The intent states the conformance rule "every number is a knob settable by file, CLI, MCP and prompt", but this module adds `MIN_DOC = 10` as a bare constant used directly in `problems()` (`len(k.doc.strip()) < MIN_DOC`), with no file/CLI/MCP/prompt source and no override path; `RETENTIONS`/`_KEYS` are likewise fixed sets. An operator who wants a stricter or looser doc-length gate (e.g. per org) cannot set it, so the ratchet threshold is not configurable as required.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/eventkinds.py:MIN_DOC

chunk_findings.detail: `_declare` recreates the unreleased upgrade fragment for any kind whose `event_kind_added.<kind>.toml` is absent, with no `_released(kind)` guard, even though `check` right below treats that fragment as unnecessary for a released kind (`... and not _released(kind)`). This is reachable exactly through the workflow the new ratchet creates: once `check` prints `registry: declared in no ddflow/templates/events/<owner>.toml` for a kind that already shipped, the tool that fixes `check` output is `add`. Given a kind such as `task.created` that was released earlier (its fragment was folded into that release, so `_released("task.created")` is true and the file is gone), running `uv run scripts/event_kind.py add task.created --why "<long doc>"` takes the `if not frag.exists()` branch and writes a fresh `ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/event_kind_added.task.created.toml` (nothing else is needed if the registry row is already present). Since `check` only reports *missing* fragments, the extra file passes validation silently, and when the next version is cut the upgrade tooling folds it into that release and announces `event_kind_added` for a kind that had already shipped in an earlier version — a wrong changelog entry produced by the tool meant to keep the registry honest.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/event_kind.py:_declare

chunk_findings.detail:
The new one-line guard is `if "|" in k.doc or "
" in k.doc.strip():` — it checks for newlines in the *stripped* doc. `str.strip()` removes leading/trailing whitespace, so a doc with a leading or trailing newline passes validation yet is still interpolated verbatim by `table()` as `f"| ... | {k.doc} |"`. Concretely, an owner file with `doc = """Records x.
"""` (TOML preserves the newline before the closing `"""`; a basic string `"Records x.
"` is equivalent) yields `k.doc == "Records x.
"`; `k.doc.strip()` is `"Records x."`, which ends with `.` and contains no newline, so `problems()` returns no line for this kind. The generated docs table then emits `| \`x.y\` | owner | 1 | keep | Records x.` followed by a stray ` |` line, which terminates the Markdown table — exactly the failure the guard was added to prevent. The same applies to a leading newline (`
Records x.`), and `` is likewise removed by `strip()`. The probe added for #1 (`test_a_doc_that_would_break_the_table_is_refused`) apparently exercises `|`, not this path, so it does not answer it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/eventkinds.py:problems

chunk_findings.detail: The previous review's [r-everything-configurable] finding on `MIN_DOC` still holds: the number is now defined as a bare constant in `scripts/event_kind.py` (`MIN_DOC = 10`) with no file/CLI/MCP/prompt source, rather than being made a knob — it was moved out of `ddflow/core/eventkinds.py` (where the constants ratchet flags it) instead of being fixed. Worse, the script only enforces it on the `add --why` path, while `problems()` lost the `len(k.doc.strip()) < MIN_DOC` check entirely, so the declaration-file path the intent names as the primary one now accepts `doc = "x."` (two characters, ends with a full stop) and `check`/`problems()` report nothing. Any numbers rule that must be settable per project/org cannot be satisfied by a literal in a script that is bypassed by hand-edited owner files.
